content: 1. If serologic testing is not feasible, the vaccine dose should be repeated unless testing confirms an adequate immune response to the vaccine. The repeat dose or serologic testing should be performed after the interval recommended for the antibody-containing product. 2. Although passively acquired antibodies can interfere with the immune response to the rubella vaccine, the low dose of anti-Rho(D) globulin administered to postpartum women has not been shown to reduce the immune response to the RA 27/3 strain rubella vaccine. 3. Due to the critical importance of rubella and varicella immunity among women of childbearing age, postpartum vaccination with MMR, varicella, or MMRV vaccines should not be delayed because of the receipt of anti-Rho(D) globulin or any other blood product during the last trimester of pregnancy or at delivery. 4. Women without evidence of immunity to rubella or varicella should be vaccinated immediately after giving birth. If possible, they should be tested more than three months later to confirm immunity to rubella and, if appropriate, to measles. 5. Interference with vaccine efficacy may occur if an antibody-containing product is administered shortly after MMR or varicella vaccines. Vaccine virus replication and immune stimulation typically occur within 1–2 weeks after vaccination. 6. If an antibody-containing product is administered within 14 days of vaccination with MMR or varicella vaccines, the vaccination should be repeated after the recommended interval unless serologic testing confirms a protective antibody response. 7. A humanized monoclonal antibody product (palivizumab) is available as prophylaxis for serious lower respiratory tract disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants and young children. This product contains only antibodies to RSV and does not interfere with the immune response to licensed live or inactivated vaccines. 8. Antibody-containing products interact less with inactivated vaccines, toxoids, recombinant subunit, and polysaccharide vaccines compared to live vaccines. Administering inactivated vaccines and toxoids either simultaneously with or at any interval before or after receiving an antibody-containing product does not significantly impair the development of a protective antibody response. 9. Inactivated vaccines or toxoids and antibody preparations should be administered at different anatomical sites using the standard recommended dose. Increasing the vaccine dose volume or the number of vaccinations is neither indicated nor recommended. 10. Certain vaccines that protect against the same diseases are available from different manufacturers and may differ in antigen content, amount, or formulation method. Manufacturers use different production processes, and their products may contain varying concentrations of antigen per dose or different stabilizers or preservatives. 11. Available data suggest that infants who receive sequential doses of different Hib conjugate, hepatitis B, and hepatitis A vaccines produce a satisfactory antibody response after completing the primary series. All brands of Hib conjugate, hepatitis B, hepatitis A, rotavirus, and quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccines are interchangeable within their respective series. 12. For the first three doses of the DTaP series, data indicate that one or two doses of Tripedia (Sanofi Pasteur) followed by Infanrix (GlaxoSmithKline) for the remaining dose(s) produce comparable immunogenicity to three doses of Tripedia, as measured by antibodies to diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis toxoids, and filamentous hemagglutinin. 13. However, in the absence of a clear serologic correlate of protection for pertussis, the relevance of these immunogenicity data for protection against pertussis is unknown. When feasible, the same brand of DTaP vaccine should be used for all doses in the vaccination series. 14. If vaccination providers do not know or have access to the type of DTaP vaccine previously administered to a child, any DTaP vaccine may be used to continue or complete the series. 15. For a child requiring two doses of influenza vaccine (TIV or LAIV), it is preferable to use the same type of vaccine for both doses.
